q0: import math as m imports math under the name m only. The name math is never created, so math.pi → NameError. Use m.pi.
q1: Python runs top to bottom. from math import pi creates pi = 3.14159…, then pi = 3 overwrites it. The last assignment wins → 3.
q2: This time your pi = 3 comes first, then the import overwrites it with math's pi (3.14159…). int(3.14159… * 100) = int(314.159…) = 314.
q3: from module import * imports every public name, but skips names starting with an underscore (_x). They are treated as private.
q4: dir(module) gives a list of all the names inside the module, sorted alphabetically. The module must be imported with import math first.
q5: On −2.5: floor goes down → −3. ceil goes up → −2. trunc cuts the decimals, moving toward 0 → −2. For negatives, trunc behaves like ceil.
q6: sqrt and hypot always return floats: √16 = 4.0 and √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10.0. That's why the answer has decimals.
q7: ceil, floor, trunc and factorial return int. sqrt always returns float, even for a perfect square like 4.
q8: factorial only works on non-negative whole numbers. −3 is a valid int (so not TypeError) but an invalid value → ValueError.
q9: randint(a, b) includes both ends, so 10 is possible. randrange(1, 10) stops at 9 (end excluded). randrange(10) gives 0–9. random() is always < 1.0.
q10: sample picks unique elements. You can't pick 6 different items from only 5 → ValueError (sample larger than population).
q11: randrange(1) means 0 up to 1, with 1 excluded. The only possible value is 0, every time.
q12: A seed fixes the starting point of the random generator. The same seed always produces the same sequence, on every run.
q13: python_version_tuple() returns a tuple of 3 strings, like ('3', '12', '4'). So v[0] is a str and the length is 3.
q14: processor() gives the real CPU name. machine() only gives the generic type (e.g. x86_64). system() is the OS name.
q15: A module's code runs only at its first import. Python remembers it and skips every later import of the same module.
q16: The first import runs the module and prints 'loaded'. The second one is silently skipped. Then counter_mod.n is 1 → loaded, then 1.
q17: A file that is run directly always has __name__ == '__main__'. Only when it is imported does __name__ become the module's name ('tool').
q18: sys.path is the list of folders searched during an import, in order. The first one is the folder of the script you started.
q19: .pyc files hold semi-compiled bytecode, which makes the next import faster. It's not machine code: the Python interpreter still runs it.
q20: In the course, a folder becomes a package when it contains __init__.py. That file runs when the package is first imported.
q21: Importing shop.cart first runs shop/__init__.py (prints 'init'). Then the full path shop.cart.total() works → init, 5.
q22: import shop.cart defines only the name shop. The bare name cart doesn't exist: 'init' prints, then NameError. Write shop.cart.total() or use from shop import cart.
q23: -U (or --upgrade) tells pip install to update a package that's already installed. There is no pip upgrade command.
q24: pip show name prints a package's details, including Requires: (its dependencies). pip list lists all installed packages.
q25: ord('A') = 65 (uppercase letters start at 65; 'a' is 97). chr(98) is the character with code 98 = 'b'.
q26: UCS-4 is fixed width: always 32 bits = 4 bytes per character. Simple, but wasteful for plain English text.
q27: UTF-8 is variable width: 1 to 4 bytes, as many as each character needs. ASCII characters take just 1 byte.
q28: Between the triple quotes there is only the line break. A line break is one character (\n) → length 1.
q29: 'python' has indexes p0 y1 t2 h3 o4 n5. [1:4] → indexes 1, 2, 3 = 'yth'. [-2:] → 'on'. [::-2] starts at the end and takes every 2nd: n, h, y → 'nhy'.
q30: Strings are immutable: you can never change a character in place. s[1] = 'X' → TypeError. Build a new string instead: s[:1] + 'X' + s[2:].
q31: Same reason: strings are immutable, so you can't delete a character → TypeError. (del s, which deletes the whole variable, is allowed.)
q32: min/max compare code points. In 'Hello world' the space (32) is the smallest, so min is ' '. In 'Hello' the letters are H(72) e(101) l(108) o(111) → max 'o'.
q33: b0 a1 n2 a3 n4 a5. find gives the first 'na' → 2. rfind gives the last one → 4. Not found → −1 (no error).
q34: index() works like find(), but when nothing is found it raises ValueError instead of returning −1.
q35: capitalize: first character up, all the rest lower → 'Abc'. title: each word starts upper, rest lower → 'Abc Def'. swapcase flips each letter → 'hI'.
q36: Every isxxx() is False on the empty string. 'abc1' is all letters and digits → True. '3.5' contains a dot, which isn't a digit → False.
q37: isupper/islower only check the letters: 'ABC 12' → True, 'abc' → True. ' \t' is a space and a tab, both whitespace → True.
q38: strip() removes spaces on both sides → 'hi', then + '|' gives 'hi|'. rstrip('x') removes x's on the right only → 'xxhi'.
q39: split() with no argument splits on any run of whitespace and drops empty pieces. split(',') keeps the empty string between the two commas.
q40: sep.join(items) puts the separator between items, never at the ends → 'x-y-z'. A string is a sequence of characters, so '+'.join('ab') → 'a+b'.
q41: join only accepts strings. The list contains ints → TypeError. Fix: ','.join(map(str, [1, 2])).
q42: replace('a', 'b', 2) replaces only the first 2 matches → 'bba'. 'tic tac' contains 't' twice → 2.
q43: upper() returns a new string, and here it isn't stored anywhere. Strings are immutable, so s is still 'hey'. You'd need s = s.upper().
q44: 'ab' is 2 characters and the width is 6, so there are 4 '*' to add, split evenly: 2 left and 2 right → '**ab**'.
q45: Strings compare character by character by code point. 'a' < 'b' → True. 'Z' (90) < 'a' (97): uppercase comes first → True. 'abc' < 'ab' → False: the shorter one ('ab') is the smaller.
q46: '10' < '9' compares characters: '1' < '9' → True (text, not numbers!). A str and an int are never equal → '10' == 10 is False.
q47: < and > between a str and an int are not allowed → TypeError. Only == and != work between them (always False and always True).
q48: lst.sort() sorts the list in place and returns None. The print shows None, then the now-sorted list ['a', 'b'].
q49: sorted() on a string returns a list of characters, sorted by code point. Uppercase comes before lowercase → ['A', 'b', 'c'].
q50: int() on a string accepts only a whole number written as text. '7.0' has a dot → ValueError. int(float('7.0')) would work.
q51: The except branches are checked top to bottom, and the first match wins. ZeroDivisionError is an ArithmeticError, so the first branch catches it → 'A'. The second branch can never run.
q52: int('a') fails right away, so 'ok' is never printed. The ValueError branch prints 'V'. The error was handled, so the program continues → 'end'.
q53: [1][2] → IndexError, which is in the tuple (KeyError, IndexError) → 'caught'. Only one branch ever runs.
q54: The bare except: catches everything, so it must be the last branch. If you put it earlier, Python refuses to run: SyntaxError.
q55: The IndexError raised inside f() isn't handled there, so it travels up to the caller. IndexError is a subclass of LookupError → 'L'.
q56: KeyboardInterrupt (Ctrl-C) inherits directly from BaseException, not from Exception. That's why except Exception doesn't catch Ctrl-C.
q57: LookupError is a category (abstract): it's the parent of IndexError and KeyError. The other three are concrete errors that actually get raised.
q58: KeyError's parent is LookupError → True. ValueError is not under ArithmeticError (its parent is Exception) → False.
q59: 1E250 is a float. Squaring it gives 1E500, which is too big for a float → OverflowError. (Big ints never overflow.)
q60: A bare raise re-raises the exception being handled right now. Here there is none, so Python raises RuntimeError instead (caught by except Exception).
q61: Inside f, the except prints 'inner', then the bare raise sends the same ZeroDivisionError up to the caller, which prints 'outer'.
q62: assert 0 fails, because 0 is false. The text after the comma becomes the error message, so print(e) → 'zero!'.
q63: assert only fails on false values (0, '', [], None, False). 'x' is a non-empty string, so it's true → the assert passes and 'passed' is printed.
q64: No error happened, so except is skipped and else runs → 'L'. finally always runs → 'F'.
q65: finally runs even after return 'T'. Its own return 'F' replaces the first return value → 'F'.
q66: There's no except branch, so the error isn't handled. finally still runs first ('cleanup'), then the ZeroDivisionError continues and stops the program.
q67: e.args is a tuple of all the arguments given to the exception → ('a', 'b').
q68: With no arguments, args is the empty tuple () and str(e) is the empty string ''.
q69: except Exception also catches MyErr (its child). type(e).__name__ is the real class name, 'MyErr', and print(e) shows the message 'boom'.
q70: We raise an A. except B doesn't match: an A is not a B (B is the child, not the parent). except A matches → 'A'.
q71: Calling A().hi() makes Python pass the object automatically as the first argument. hi() has no parameter to receive it → TypeError. Methods need self.
q72: P() uses the default x = 2. P(5) sets x = 5. 2 + 5 = 7.
q73: Each object gets its own list from __init__. a gets 2 pushes, b gets 1 → 2 1.
q74: The constructor is always named __init__. Python calls it automatically when you create an object.
q75: __x is private: inside the class it was renamed to _A__x. From outside, __x doesn't exist → AttributeError.
q76: Name mangling: __x written inside class A becomes _A__x. Using that full name from outside works → 1.
q77: __x was written inside the class → mangled to _A__x. __y was created from outside → not mangled, it stays '__y'.
q78: Inside the class, the private name works normally. self.__m() is automatically mangled to _B__m too, so it finds the method → 'm'.
q79: n is a class variable (one shared copy). Each constructor call adds 1 → two objects → 2.
q80: a.v = 9 creates a new instance variable in a only, hiding the class one. b and C still see the class variable → 9 1 1.
q81: a has no own v, so reading a.v falls back to the class variable, which was changed to 5 → 5.
q82: append changes the one shared list. No assignment happened, so no instance variable was created → b sees [1].
q83: c.__dict__ holds only the object's own variables: {'m': 4}. The class variable k lives in C.__dict__ → True.
q84: x is a class variable: visible from the class and its objects. y is created in __init__, so only objects have it, not the class → True False True.
q85: A.__name__ → 'A'. type(A()) is A, so its name is 'A'. __module__ is the module where A was defined: '__main__' for the file you run.
q86: Objects don't have __name__; only classes (and functions/modules) do → AttributeError. Use type(obj).__name__.
q87: __bases__ is a tuple of the direct parents, in the order written: A, B. A has no written parent, so its base is object.
q88: With n = −1, the if is false, so self.pos is never created. Reading it → AttributeError.
q89: B's __init__ never calls A's, so self.a is never created → AttributeError. Fix: add super().__init__().
q90: super().__init__(10) runs A's constructor with n = 10. Note there's no self when you use super() → 10.
q91: A.f(self) calls the parent's version (returns 'A'), then 'B' is added → 'AB'.
q92: b is a B, and B is a child of A → isinstance(b, A) True. An A object is not a B → False. Every class is a subclass of itself → True.
q93: y = x doesn't copy: both names point to the same object, so changing y.v changes x.v → 2. x is y → True. z is a different object, even with the same value → False.
q94: C(A, B) searches its parents left to right: A first, and A has x → 'A'.
q95: The MRO of D(B, C) is D, B, C, A. B has no f, and C has one before A is reached → 'C'.
q96: B(T, M) lists T before its own child M. Python can't build a consistent search order → TypeError. Write B(M, T).
q97: C has no v, so the search goes to B (v = 2) → 2. C.__mro__ is (C, B, A, object), so index 1 is B.
q98: run() calls self.kind(). For a P object that's P's kind → 'P'. For a Q object, Q's override runs → 'Q'. The object decides (polymorphism).
q99: B doesn't define __str__, so it inherits A's. print(B()) calls it → 'I am A'.
q100: __str__ must return a string. Returning 1 makes print fail → TypeError.
q101: Overriding = a subclass redefines a method that already exists in its superclass, using the same name.
q102: Course definition: every object has a name (to identify it), a set of properties (data) and a set of methods (actions).
q103: Each next() runs the generator until the next yield: the first gives 1, the second gives 2.
q104: The generator has only one yield. The first next returns 'a'; the second finds nothing left → StopIteration.
q105: list(x) uses up the generator → [0, 1, 4]. A generator works only once, so the second list is empty: [].
q106: Calling g() only creates the generator; its body doesn't run until next(). So 'A' is never printed, only 'B'.
q107: Parentheses make a generator expression, not a tuple. sum uses it up: 0 + 1 + 2 = 3.
q108: The if at the end filters: keep n from 0 to 7 when n % 3 == 0 → 0, 3, 6.
q109: The if … else comes before for, so every item is kept, but transformed: odd n (n % 2 is 1, true) stays n, even n becomes '-' → ['-', 1, '-', 3].
q110: Two for clauses work like nested loops: the first is the outer one. For 'x' it goes through '1', '2', then the same for 'y'.
q112: [[]] * 3 is a list holding 3 (identical) empty lists → length 3. The comprehension builds a fresh [0, 0] for each of the 2 characters.
q114: (lambda: 'hi')() defines the lambda and calls it right away → 'hi'. 2 * 'x' repeats the string → 'xx'.
q115: map applies x * 2 to every element; list() turns the map object into a list → [2, 4, 6].
q116: map returns a lazy map object (an iterator), not a list. Printing it shows something like <map object at 0x…>. Wrap it in list() to see the values.
q117: filter keeps only the items where the lambda returns True: length > 2 → 'abc' and 'abcd'.
q118: With two lists, map takes one item from each and stops at the shortest list: 10−1 = 9, 20−2 = 18 (30 has no partner).
q119: The key is −len, so the longest strings get the smallest key and come first → ['ccc', 'bb', 'a'].
q121: Each lambda looks up k when it is called, not when it was created. By then the loop has finished with k = 2, so every lambda returns 2.
q122: The closure remembers msg, so f() → 'hi'. But msg isn't a global name, so print(msg) → NameError.
q123: Mode 'r' is the default, and the file must exist → FileNotFoundError (a subclass of OSError, also known as IOError).
q124: 'a' = append: keeps the old content and writes at the end, creating the file if needed. 'w' would erase everything first.
q125: At the end of a file, readline() returns the empty string ''. That's how loops know to stop. No exception is raised.
q126: readlines() returns a list of lines, and each line keeps its ' ' → ['a ', 'b '].
q128: print() writes to sys.stdout (the screen). Errors go to sys.stderr, and input() reads from sys.stdin.
q129: Every OS error carries an errno number. A missing file has errno.ENOENT ('No such file or directory') → True.
q131: Each byte must be between 0 and 255. 300 is an int but out of range → ValueError.
q132: A bytearray only stores ints. 'x' is a string → TypeError.
q133: weekday() counts Monday = 0 … Sunday = 6. January 1, 2024 was a Monday → 0. (isoweekday() would give 1.)
q134: A timedelta prints as 'days, H:MM:SS' → '1 day, 3:00:00'.
q135: Leap-year rule: divisible by 4, except centuries, unless divisible by 400. 1900 is a century not divisible by 400 → False. 2000 is divisible by 400 → True.
q136: The loop ends normally (no break), so the else runs. The loop variable keeps its last value, 2.
q137: break at i == 1 skips the loop's else. Only print(i) runs → 1.
q138: 3 doesn't match 1 | 2. case _ is the default that matches anything → 'big'.
q139: The default list bag=[] is created once, when the function is defined, and shared by every call. The first call left 1 in it → [1, 2].
q140: {…} with one expression is a set: duplicates vanish → {0, 1}. With key: value it's a dict: each letter maps to itself doubled.
q141: For 'docs/a.txt': suffix is the extension with its dot ('.txt'), stem is the name without the extension ('a'), name is the full file name ('a.txt').
q142: A logic error gives no error message: the code runs, but the result is wrong. Syntax errors stop the program before it runs; runtime errors raise exceptions.
q143: Human-in-the-loop: a person reviews, tests and approves what the AI produces before it's used. You stay responsible for it.
q144: When two branches change the same lines differently, Git can't choose → merge conflict. A person decides the final version.
